content: Endometriosis is a prevalent gynecological condition that affects 6% to 11% of women of reproductive age. It is associated with symptoms such as painful intercourse (dyspareunia), painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea), and infertility. One therapeutic approach involves the use of gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRHas), which aim to alleviate pain caused by endometriosis. However, a notable adverse effect of GnRHas is a reduction in bone mineral density (BMD). This review not only assessed the impact of GnRHas on pain relief, quality of life, and patient satisfaction but also evaluated their effects on BMD and the risk of adverse events compared to other treatment options. The objective of this review was to determine the effectiveness and safety of GnRHas in managing painful symptoms of endometriosis and to assess their impact on BMD in affected women. A comprehensive search was conducted in May 2022 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group trials register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, as well as trial registries. Additional studies were identified through reference checking and consultation with experts in the field. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared GnRHas with other hormonal treatments, such as analgesics, danazol, intrauterine progestogens, oral or injectable progestogens, and gestrinone. Trials comparing GnRHas alone versus GnRHas combined with add-back therapy (hormonal or non-hormonal) or calcium-regulating agents were also included. Standard Cochrane methodology was employed for data collection and analysis. The primary outcomes were overall pain relief and objective measurements of BMD. Secondary outcomes included adverse effects, quality of life, improvement in the most troublesome symptoms, and patient satisfaction. Due to a high risk of bias in some studies, primary analyses were restricted to studies with a low risk of selection bias, followed by sensitivity analyses that included all studies. A total of 72 studies involving 7,355 participants were included in the review. The quality of evidence was rated as very low to low, primarily due to significant risks of bias and imprecision in the studies. Findings from the trials: 1. GnRHas versus no treatment: No studies were identified comparing GnRHas with no treatment. 2. GnRHas versus placebo: Treatment with GnRHas may reduce overall pain, as indicated by pelvic pain scores (relative risk [RR] 2.14; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.41 to 3.24, 1 RCT, n = 87, low-certainty evidence), dysmenorrhea scores (RR 2.25; 95% CI 1.59 to 3.16, 1 RCT, n = 85, low-certainty evidence), dyspareunia scores (RR 2.21; 95% CI 1.39 to 3.54, 1 RCT, n = 59, low-certainty evidence), and pelvic tenderness scores (RR 2.28; 95% CI 1.48 to 3.50, 1 RCT, n = 85, low-certainty evidence) after three months of treatment. The effect on pelvic induration was uncertain (RR 1.07; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.79, 1 RCT, n = 81, low-certainty evidence). GnRHas may be associated with a higher incidence of hot flushes after three months of treatment (RR 3.08; 95% CI 1.89 to 5.01, 1 RCT, n = 100, low-certainty evidence). 3. GnRHas versus danazol: The effect of GnRHas compared to danazol on overall pain relief was uncertain, with very low-certainty evidence for outcomes such as pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, pelvic induration, and pelvic tenderness after three months of treatment. After six months of treatment, there may be a slight reduction in pelvic pain (mean difference [MD] 0.50; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.90, 1 RCT, n = 41, very low-certainty evidence) and pelvic induration (MD 0.70; 95% CI 0.21 to 1.19, 1 RCT, n = 41, very low-certainty evidence) with GnRHas compared to danazol. 4. GnRHas versus analgesics: No studies were identified comparing GnRHas with analgesics. 5. GnRHas versus intrauterine progestogens: No studies with a low risk of bias were identified for this comparison. 6. GnRHas versus GnRHas combined with calcium-regulating agents: Treatment with GnRHas alone may result in a slight decrease in BMD after 12 months compared to GnRHas combined with calcium-regulating agents. This was observed for the anterior-posterior spine (MD -7.00; 95% CI -7.53 to -6.47, 1 RCT, n = 41, very low-certainty evidence) and the lateral spine (MD -12.40; 95% CI -13.31 to -11.49, 1 RCT, n = 41, very low-certainty evidence). Conclusions: GnRHas may provide slight pain relief compared to placebo or oral/injectable progestogens. However, the evidence is uncertain when comparing GnRHas with danazol, intrauterine progestogens, or gestrinone. GnRHas may lead to a slight reduction in BMD compared to gestrinone and a more significant reduction in BMD compared to GnRHas combined with calcium-regulating agents. Adverse effects, such as hot flushes, may be more common with GnRHas compared to placebo or gestrinone. Given the very low to low certainty of the evidence and variability in outcome measures, these findings should be interpreted with caution.
